claim: Primary sensory areas of cortex compute sensorimotor prediction errors based on deviations between predictions and actual sensory input.
source: Based on deviations between predictions and actual sensory input, primary sensory areas of cortex have been shown to compute sensorimotor prediction errors.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work on prediction errors in cortex

claim: L2/3 neurons in mouse auditory cortex respond to sounds.
source: We first assessed population responses of L2/3 neurons evoked by sounds (pure tones presented at 4, 8, 16, or 32 kHz at either 60 or 75 dB sound pressure level [SPL]; Figure 1F) presented while the VR was off.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing neuronal responses to pure tones

claim: Pure tones resulted in both increases and decreases in calcium activity in individual L2/3 ACx neurons.
source: While pure tones resulted in both increases and decreases in calcium activity in individual neurons (Figure 1G), the average population response exhibited a significant decrease in activity (Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data showing diverse responses

claim: The average population response of L2/3 ACx neurons to pure tones exhibited a significant decrease in activity.
source: While pure tones resulted in both increases and decreases in calcium activity in individual neurons (Figure 1G), the average population response exhibited a significant decrease in activity (Figure 1H).
evidence: Supported by population-level calcium imaging data

claim: L2/3 neurons in mouse auditory cortex respond to visual stimuli.
source: Next, we analyzed visual responses evoked by full-field drifting gratings (see Methods; Figure 1I). Visual stimulation resulted in a diverse response across the population of L2/3 neurons (Figure 1J) that was initially positive at the population level (Figure 1K).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing neuronal responses to visual gratings

claim: Visual stimulation resulted in a diverse response across the population of L2/3 ACx neurons.
source: Visual stimulation resulted in a diverse response across the population of L2/3 neurons (Figure 1J) that was initially positive at the population level (Figure 1K).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data showing varied responses

claim: The average population response of L2/3 ACx neurons to visual stimulation was initially positive.
source: Visual stimulation resulted in a diverse response across the population of L2/3 neurons (Figure 1J) that was initially positive at the population level (Figure 1K).
evidence: Supported by population-level calcium imaging data

claim: L2/3 neurons in mouse auditory cortex respond to running onsets.
source: To quantify motor-related inputs, we analyzed activity during running onsets collected across all experimental conditions (Figure 1L). We found that the majority of neurons increased their activity during running onsets (Figure 1M), which was also reflected in a significant positive response on the population level (Figure 1N).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing neuronal responses to running onsets

claim: The majority of L2/3 ACx neurons increased their activity during running onsets.
source: We found that the majority of neurons increased their activity during running onsets (Figure 1M), which was also reflected in a significant positive response on the population level (Figure 1N).
evidence: Supported by calcium imaging data showing increased activity

claim: Running onsets resulted in a significant positive response at the population level in L2/3 ACx.
source: We found that the majority of neurons increased their activity during running onsets (Figure 1M), which was also reflected in a significant positive response on the population level (Figure 1N).
evidence: Supported by population-level calcium imaging data

claim: Running modulates auditory responses in ACx in a variety of different ways.
source: In ACx running has been shown to modulate auditory responses in a variety of different ways (Audette et al., 2022; Bigelow et al., 2019; Henschke et al., 2021; McGinley et al., 2015; Morandell et al., 2023; Schneider et al., 2014; Vivaldo et al., 2023; Yavorska and Wehr, 2021; Zhou et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple prior studies

claim: Running strongly increases responses to visual stimuli in V1.
source: In V1, running strongly increases responses to visual stimuli (Niell and Stryker, 2010), while in ACx running has been shown to modulate auditory responses in a variety of different ways (Audette et al., 2022; Bigelow et al., 2019; Henschke et al., 2021; McGinley et al., 2015; Morandell et al., 2023; Schneider et al., 2014; Vivaldo et al., 2023; Yavorska and Wehr, 2021; Zhou et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work

claim: Sound-evoked responses of ACx neurons were overall similar during sitting and running, but exhibited a smaller decrease in activity when the mouse was sitting.
source: Separating auditory responses by running state, we found that sound-evoked responses of ACx neurons were overall similar during sitting and running, but exhibited a smaller decrease in activity when the mouse was sitting (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing responses during different behavioral states

claim: Visual responses in ACx consisted of an increase of activity during running and a decrease of activity during sitting.
source: Visual responses consisted of an increase of activity during running, and a decrease of activity during sitting (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing responses during different behavioral states

claim: The running modulation effect on visual responses in ACx is reminiscent of that observed in V1.
source: This is reminiscent of the running modulation effect observed on visual responses in V1 (Niell and Stryker, 2010).
evidence: Supported by comparison to cited prior work

claim: Running appears to moderately and differentially modulate auditory and visual responses in L2/3 ACx neurons.
source: Thus, running appears to moderately and differentially modulate auditory and visual responses in L2/3 ACx neurons.
evidence: Inferred from the differential effects of running on auditory vs visual responses

claim: Running modulation influences L2/3 ACx neurons differently than in V1.
source: Consistent with previous work, these results demonstrate that auditory, visual, and motor-related signals are all present in ACx and that running modulation influences L2/3 ACx neurons differently than in V1.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of running effects in ACx vs V1

claim: Auditory, visual, and motor-related signals are all present in ACx.
source: Consistent with previous work, these results demonstrate that auditory, visual, and motor-related signals are all present in ACx and that running modulation influences L2/3 ACx neurons differently than in V1.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing responses to all three types of stimuli

claim: L2/3 neurons in ACx respond to audiomotor (AM) mismatches.
source: We found that AM mismatch resulted in a strong population response (Figure 2C, D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing neuronal responses to AM mismatches

claim: AM mismatch resulted in a strong population response in L2/3 ACx.
source: We found that AM mismatch resulted in a strong population response (Figure 2C, D).
evidence: Supported by population-level calcium imaging data

claim: AM mismatch responses likely cannot be attributed to changes in running speed.
source: AM mismatch responses likely cannot be attributed to changes in running speed and do not result in a pupil response. We found no evidence of AM mismatch induced changes in running speed (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) or pupil dilation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing no changes in running speed or pupil dilation

claim: AM mismatch responses do not result in a pupil response.
source: AM mismatch responses likely cannot be attributed to changes in running speed and do not result in a pupil response. We found no evidence of AM mismatch induced changes in running speed (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A) or pupil dilation (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing no pupil dilation

claim: The AM mismatch response was already apparent in the first closed loop session with AM coupling that the mice ever experienced.
source: Interestingly, the AM mismatch response was already apparent in the first closed loop session with AM coupling that the mice ever experienced, suggesting that this coupling is learned very rapidly (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from first exposure sessions

claim: The AM coupling is learned very rapidly.
source: Interestingly, the AM mismatch response was already apparent in the first closed loop session with AM coupling that the mice ever experienced, suggesting that this coupling is learned very rapidly (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Inferred from the presence of mismatch responses in the first session

claim: The average response to the playback of sound halt during the open loop session was significantly less strong than the average response to AM mismatch.
source: The average response to the playback of sound halt during the open loop session was significantly less strong than the average response to AM mismatch (Figure 2D, for detailed discussion on the relationship between mismatch responses and offset responses, see the authors' response to reviewers' recommendations).
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing closed and open loop responses

claim: There is no evidence of a running modulation of the response to the playback halt in ACx.
source: In contrast to visual playback halt responses in V1 (Vasilevskaya et al., 2023), we found no evidence of a running modulation of the response to the playback halt (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing no difference between sitting and running

claim: Visual playback halt responses in V1 show running modulation.
source: In contrast to visual playback halt responses in V1 (Vasilevskaya et al., 2023), we found no evidence of a running modulation of the response to the playback halt (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work

claim: L2/3 neurons in ACx respond to AM mismatch in a way similar to how L2/3 neurons in V1 respond to VM mismatch.
source: Thus, L2/3 neurons in ACx respond to AM mismatch in a way similar to how the L2/3 neurons in V1 respond to VM mismatch.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of AM mismatch responses in ACx to VM mismatch responses in V1

claim: AM mismatch neurons exhibited a strong reduction in activity in response to sound stimulation.
source: Consistent with a model of a subtractive computation of prediction errors, we found that AM mismatch neurons exhibited a strong reduction in activity in response to sound stimulation and an increase of activity on running onsets (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from AM mismatch responsive neurons

claim: AM mismatch neurons exhibited an increase of activity on running onsets.
source: Consistent with a model of a subtractive computation of prediction errors, we found that AM mismatch neurons exhibited a strong reduction in activity in response to sound stimulation and an increase of activity on running onsets (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from AM mismatch responsive neurons

claim: Mismatch responses are likely enriched in the superficial part of L2/3.
source: Given that mismatch responses are likely enriched in the superficial part of L2/3 (O'Toole et al., 2023), and that in our two-photon imaging experiments we also preferentially recorded from more superficial neurons, we suspect that our population is enriched for mismatch neurons.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work

claim: The recorded population is enriched for mismatch neurons.
source: Given that mismatch responses are likely enriched in the superficial part of L2/3 (O'Toole et al., 2023), and that in our two-photon imaging experiments we also preferentially recorded from more superficial neurons, we suspect that our population is enriched for mismatch neurons.
evidence: Inferred from recording location and prior knowledge about mismatch neuron distribution

claim: Sound-evoked responses were significantly more negative in neurons strongly responsive to AM mismatch than for the remainder of the L2/3 neuronal population.
source: Nevertheless, sound-evoked responses were significantly more negative in neurons strongly responsive to AM mismatch, than for the remainder of the L2/3 neuronal population (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing subpopulations

claim: The correlation of calcium activity of AM mismatch neurons was predominantly negative with sound amplitude and positive with running speed in open loop sessions.
source: Consistent with a sound driven reduction of activity and running related increase of activity in AM mismatch neurons, the correlation of calcium activity of AM mismatch neurons was predominantly negative with sound amplitude and positive with running speed in open loop sessions (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing correlations

claim: The properties of AM mismatch neurons in ACx resemble the properties of VM mismatch neurons in V1.
source: This again resembles the properties of VM mismatch neurons in V1 (Attinger et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by comparison to cited prior work

claim: There is a positive correlation between AM mismatch responses and playback sound halt responses for all neurons.
source: When comparing AM mismatch responses with playback sound halt responses for all neurons, we do indeed find a positive correlation between the two (Figure 2—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing correlation

claim: In closed loop running onsets in which the sound was coupled to movement, only a transient running onset response was observed.
source: In closed loop running onsets in which the sound was coupled to movement, we indeed observed only a transient running onset response (Figure 2H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from closed loop sessions

claim: In the open loop condition, running onset responses were sustained.
source: In contrast, in the open loop condition, running onset responses were sustained, possibly reflecting motor-related input that is not cancelled out by sensory input.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from open loop sessions

claim: Sustained running onset responses in open loop possibly reflect motor-related input that is not cancelled out by sensory input.
source: In contrast, in the open loop condition, running onset responses were sustained, possibly reflecting motor-related input that is not cancelled out by sensory input.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the sustained responses

claim: The difference in input processing depends on whether the animal is in the coupled or uncoupled condition.
source: This analysis highlights the difference in input processing depending on whether the animal is in the coupled or uncoupled condition and is consistent with subtractive interactions between prediction and sensory signals.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of closed and open loop responses

claim: The results are consistent with subtractive interactions between prediction and sensory signals.
source: This analysis highlights the difference in input processing depending on whether the animal is in the coupled or uncoupled condition and is consistent with subtractive interactions between prediction and sensory signals.
evidence: Inferred from the pattern of responses in different conditions

claim: The implementation of sensorimotor prediction error computation generalizes beyond V1 to other primary cortices.
source: Overall, these results suggest that the implementation of sensorimotor prediction error computation generalizes beyond V1 to other primary cortices and might be a canonical cortical computation in L2/3.
evidence: Inferred from the similarity of AM mismatch responses in ACx to VM mismatch responses in V1

claim: Sensorimotor prediction error computation might be a canonical cortical computation in L2/3.
source: Overall, these results suggest that the implementation of sensorimotor prediction error computation generalizes beyond V1 to other primary cortices and might be a canonical cortical computation in L2/3.
evidence: Speculative generalization from the observed pattern

claim: Neither VM mismatches nor visual flow playback halts resulted in a measurable population response in ACx.
source: We found that neither VM mismatches nor visual flow playback halts, which the mouse experienced in open loop sessions, resulted in a measurable population response in ACx (Figure 3C, D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing no population response

claim: No significant changes in locomotion speed were detected upon VM mismatch presentation.
source: No significant changes in locomotion speed (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) or pupil diameter (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) were detected upon VM mismatch presentation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing no changes

claim: No significant changes in pupil diameter were detected upon VM mismatch presentation.
source: No significant changes in locomotion speed (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A) or pupil diameter (Figure 3—figure supplement 1B) were detected upon VM mismatch presentation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing no changes

claim: Neurons with the strongest responses to VM mismatches exhibited positive responses to running onset and no significant response to grating stimuli.
source: Selecting the 5% of neurons with the strongest responses to VM mismatches and quantifying their responses to grating presentations and running onsets, we found that these neurons exhibited positive responses to running onset and no significant response to grating stimuli (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data from VM mismatch responsive neurons

claim: VM mismatch responsive neuron responses were not different from the population responses of the remainder of the neurons.
source: These responses were not different from the population responses of the remainder of the neurons (Figure 3F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing subpopulations

claim: VM mismatch responsive neurons exhibited a distribution not different from chance in correlation of calcium activity with visual flow speed and running speed.
source: Quantifying the correlation of calcium activity with visual flow speed and running speed in the open loop session, we found that VM mismatch responsive neurons exhibited a distribution not different from chance (Figure 3G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing random distribution

claim: Running onset responses were not different in closed and open loop conditions for VM coupling.
source: Running onset responses were not different in closed and open loop conditions (Figure 3H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing conditions

claim: Motor-related predictions are not cancelled out by visual inputs in the ACx.
source: This suggests that motor-related predictions are not cancelled out by visual inputs in the ACx.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of difference in running onset responses between closed and open loop

claim: There is no evidence of a correlation between VM mismatch responses and playback halt responses.
source: We also found no evidence of a correlation between VM mismatch responses and playback halt responses (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing no correlation

claim: There is no evidence of a VM mismatch response at the level of the L2/3 population in ACx.
source: Thus, while there may be a small subset of VM mismatch responsive neurons in L2/3 of ACx, we find no evidence of a VM mismatch response at the level of the L2/3 population.
evidence: Inferred from the lack of population-level response

claim: There may be a small subset of VM mismatch responsive neurons in L2/3 of ACx.
source: Thus, while there may be a small subset of VM mismatch responsive neurons in L2/3 of ACx, we find no evidence of a VM mismatch response at the level of the L2/3 population.
evidence: Speculative interpretation acknowledging possibility of small subset

claim: Concurrent [AM + VM] mismatch resulted in a significant response on the population level in ACx.
source: The [AM + VM] mismatch resulted in a significant response on the population level (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing population response

claim: There is no evidence of a change in running speed following [AM + VM] mismatch.
source: As with [AM] and [VM] mismatch, we found no evidence of a change in running speed or pupil diameter following [AM + VM] mismatch (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing no changes

claim: There is no evidence of a change in pupil diameter following [AM + VM] mismatch.
source: As with [AM] and [VM] mismatch, we found no evidence of a change in running speed or pupil diameter following [AM + VM] mismatch (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing no changes

claim: The presentation of a [AM + VM] mismatch led to a significantly larger response than either an [AM] or a [VM] mismatch in isolation.
source: We found that the presentation of a [AM + VM] mismatch led to a significantly larger response than either an [AM] or a [VM] mismatch in isolation (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing different mismatch conditions

claim: The concurrent presentation [AM + VM] elicited a significantly larger response than the linear sum of [AM] + [VM] mismatch responses.
source: To test whether the linear summation of [AM] + [VM] mismatch responses could explain the response to the concurrent presentation [AM + VM], we compared the two directly, and found that the concurrent presentation [AM + VM] elicited a significantly larger response than the linear sum of [AM] + [VM] mismatch responses (Figure 4E and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data comparing concurrent vs summed responses

claim: There is a subset of neurons (13.7%) that selectively respond to the concurrent [AM + VM] mismatch.
source: Plotting the [AM + VM] mismatch responses against the linear sum of the [AM] + [VM] mismatch responses for each neuron, we found that while there is some correlation between the two, there is a subset of neurons (13.7%; red dots, Figure 4F) that selectively respond to the concurrent [AM + VM] mismatch, while a different subset of neurons (11.2%; yellow dots, Figure 4F) selectively responds to the mismatch responses in isolation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing selective responses

claim: There is a subset of neurons (11.2%) that selectively responds to the mismatch responses in isolation.
source: Plotting the [AM + VM] mismatch responses against the linear sum of the [AM] + [VM] mismatch responses for each neuron, we found that while there is some correlation between the two, there is a subset of neurons (13.7%; red dots, Figure 4F) that selectively respond to the concurrent [AM + VM] mismatch, while a different subset of neurons (11.2%; yellow dots, Figure 4F) selectively responds to the mismatch responses in isolation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing selective responses

claim: Mismatch responses in different modalities can interact non-linearly.
source: This demonstrates that mismatch responses in different modalities can interact non-linearly.
evidence: Inferred from the super-additive response to concurrent mismatches

claim: AM mismatch responses were amplified when paired with concurrent VM mismatches.
source: Finally, testing for cross modal influence on AM mismatch responses by coupling both sound amplitude and visual flow speed to the speed of running, we found that AM mismatch responses were amplified when paired with concurrent VM mismatches.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing larger responses to concurrent mismatches

claim: Multimodal and non-hierarchical interactions shape prediction error responses in cortical L2/3.
source: Our results demonstrate that multimodal and non-hierarchical interactions shape prediction error responses in cortical L2/3.
evidence: Inferred from the non-linear interaction between AM and VM mismatch responses

claim: Neuronal responses consistent with prediction errors have been described in a variety of different cortical areas.
source: Neuronal responses consistent with prediction errors have been described in a variety of different cortical areas (Audette and Schneider, 2023; Ayaz et al., 2019; Han and Helmchen, 2023; Heindorf et al., 2018; Keller et al., 2012; Liu and Kanold, 2022) and across different species (Eliades and Wang, 2008; Keller and Hahnloser, 2009; Stanley and Miall, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple prior studies

claim: Neuronal responses consistent with prediction errors have been described across different species.
source: Neuronal responses consistent with prediction errors have been described in a variety of different cortical areas (Audette and Schneider, 2023; Ayaz et al., 2019; Han and Helmchen, 2023; Heindorf et al., 2018; Keller et al., 2012; Liu and Kanold, 2022) and across different species (Eliades and Wang, 2008; Keller and Hahnloser, 2009; Stanley and Miall, 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior studies in different species

claim: In V1, prediction error responses are thought to be learned with experience.
source: In V1, these responses are thought to be learned with experience (Attinger et al., 2017) and depend on local plasticity in cortex (Widmer et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: Prediction error responses in V1 depend on local plasticity in cortex.
source: In V1, these responses are thought to be learned with experience (Attinger et al., 2017) and depend on local plasticity in cortex (Widmer et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work

claim: Prediction errors signal the unanticipated appearance or absence of a sensory input.
source: Prediction errors signal the unanticipated appearance or absence of a sensory input, and are thought to be computed as a deviation between top–down predictions and bottom–up sensory inputs (Rao and Ballard, 1999).
evidence: Draws from established understanding of prediction errors

claim: Prediction errors are thought to be computed as a deviation between top–down predictions and bottom–up sensory inputs.
source: Prediction errors signal the unanticipated appearance or absence of a sensory input, and are thought to be computed as a deviation between top–down predictions and bottom–up sensory inputs (Rao and Ballard, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to theoretical framework

claim: Motor-related signals convey a prediction of sensory input.
source: One type of top–down signals that conveys a prediction of sensory input are motor-related signals (Leinweber et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work

claim: In auditory cortex, motor-related signals can modulate responses to self-generated vocalizations.
source: In auditory cortex (ACx), motor-related signals can modulate responses to self-generated vocalizations (Eliades and Wang, 2008) or to sounds coupled to locomotion (Schneider et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: In auditory cortex, motor-related signals can modulate responses to sounds coupled to locomotion.
source: In auditory cortex (ACx), motor-related signals can modulate responses to self-generated vocalizations (Eliades and Wang, 2008) or to sounds coupled to locomotion (Schneider et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work

claim: ACx is thought to use motor-related signals to compute audiomotor prediction error responses.
source: ACx is thought to use these motor-related signals to compute audiomotor (AM) prediction error responses (Audette et al., 2022; Audette and Schneider, 2023; Eliades and Wang, 2008; Keller and Hahnloser, 2009; Liu and Kanold, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple prior studies

claim: AM prediction errors can be described in a hierarchical variant of predictive processing, in which top–down motor-related signals function as predictions of bottom–up sensory input.
source: These AM prediction errors can be described in a hierarchical variant of predictive processing, in which top–down motor-related signals function as predictions of bottom–up sensory input.
evidence: Draws from theoretical framework of predictive processing

claim: Parts of both auditory and visual processing streams are well described by a hierarchy.
source: While parts of both auditory and visual processing streams are well described by a hierarchy, the cortical network as a whole does not easily map onto a hierarchical architecture, anatomically (Markov et al., 2013) or functionally (St Yves et al., 2023; Suzuki et al., 2023).
evidence: Draws from established knowledge and cited work

claim: The cortical network as a whole does not easily map onto a hierarchical architecture, anatomically or functionally.
source: While parts of both auditory and visual processing streams are well described by a hierarchy, the cortical network as a whole does not easily map onto a hierarchical architecture, anatomically (Markov et al., 2013) or functionally (St Yves et al., 2023; Suzuki et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: There is a dense reciprocal connection between ACx and V1.
source: One of the connections that does not neatly fit into a hierarchical model is the surprisingly dense reciprocal connection between ACx and V1 (Clavagnier et al., 2004; Falchier et al., 2002; Ibrahim et al., 2016; Leinweber et al., 2017; Zhao et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple prior studies

claim: The connection from ACx to V1 conveys a prediction of visual input given sound.
source: From ACx to V1, this connection conveys a prediction of visual input given sound (Garner and Keller, 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work

claim: What the reciprocal projection from V1 to ACx conveys is still unclear.
source: What the reciprocal projection from V1 to ACx conveys is still unclear.
evidence: Acknowledges gap in current knowledge

claim: In hierarchical implementations of predictive processing there are no lateral connections between primary sensory areas.
source: In proposals for hierarchical implementations of predictive processing there are no such lateral connections, and there is no reason to assume prediction error computations in different modalities should directly interact at the level of primary sensory areas.
evidence: Draws from theoretical framework of hierarchical predictive processing

claim: In hierarchical predictive processing, there is no reason to assume prediction error computations in different modalities should directly interact at the level of primary sensory areas.
source: In proposals for hierarchical implementations of predictive processing there are no such lateral connections, and there is no reason to assume prediction error computations in different modalities should directly interact at the level of primary sensory areas.
evidence: Inferred from hierarchical predictive processing theory

claim: The lateral interaction between V1 and ACx is a good starting point to investigate how non-hierarchical interactions are involved in the computation of prediction errors.
source: Thus, we argued that the lateral interaction between V1 and ACx is a good starting point to investigate how non-hierarchical interactions are involved in the computation of prediction errors, and how multimodal interactions shape sensorimotor prediction errors.
evidence: Represents the authors' reasoning for their experimental approach

claim: Auditory, visual, and motor-related signals are intermixed in the population of L2/3 neurons in ACx.
source: Consistent with previous reports, we found that auditory, visual, and motor-related signals are intermixed in the population of L2/3 neurons in ACx (Figure 1H, K, N).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and prior work

claim: Responses to motor-related signals have been reported across layers in ACx, with the strongest running modulation effect found in L2/3.
source: Responses to both motor-related (McGinley et al., 2015; Schneider et al., 2014; Vivaldo et al., 2023; Yavorska and Wehr, 2021; Zhou et al., 2014) and visual signals Bigelow et al., 2022; Morrill and Hasenstaub, 2018; Sharma et al., 2021 have been reported across layers in ACx, with the strongest running modulation effect found in L2/3 (Schneider et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work

claim: Responses to visual signals have been reported across layers in ACx.
source: Responses to both motor-related (McGinley et al., 2015; Schneider et al., 2014; Vivaldo et al., 2023; Yavorska and Wehr, 2021; Zhou et al., 2014) and visual signals Bigelow et al., 2022; Morrill and Hasenstaub, 2018; Sharma et al., 2021 have been reported across layers in ACx, with the strongest running modulation effect found in L2/3 (Schneider et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work (note: citations appear to be missing formatting in original)

claim: A subset of L2/3 neurons in ACx respond to AM prediction errors.
source: Also, consistent with previous reports, we found that a subset of L2/3 neurons in ACx respond to AM prediction errors (Figure 2C, D; Audette et al., 2022; Liu and Kanold, 2022).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citations to prior work

claim: In V1, neurons signaling prediction errors exhibit opposing influence of bottom–up visual and top–down motor-related inputs.
source: In V1, it has been demonstrated that neurons signaling prediction errors exhibit opposing influence of bottom–up visual and top–down motor-related inputs.
evidence: Draws from established findings in V1

claim: The opposing influence of bottom-up and top-down inputs in V1 prediction error neurons has been speculated to be the consequence of a subtractive computation of prediction errors.
source: This has been speculated to be the consequence of a subtractive computation of prediction errors (Jordan and Keller, 2020; Keller et al., 2012; Leinweber et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work presenting this speculation

claim: Prediction error neurons in primary ACx exhibit a positive correlation with motor-related input and a negative correlation with auditory input.
source: Our findings now reveal a similar pattern of opposing influence in prediction error neurons in primary ACx that exhibit a positive correlation with motor-related input and a negative correlation with auditory input (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing correlations

claim: The pattern of opposing influences in ACx prediction error neurons would be consistent with the idea that both VM and AM prediction errors are computed as a subtractive difference between bottom–up and top–down inputs.
source: This would be consistent with the idea that both VM and AM prediction errors are computed as a subtractive difference between bottom–up and top–down inputs.
evidence: Inferred from the observed pattern of correlations

claim: This type of computation may extend beyond primary sensory areas of cortex and may be a more general computational principle implemented in L2/3 of cortex.
source: Based on this, it is conceivable that this type of computation extends also beyond primary sensory areas of cortex and may be a more general computational principle implemented in L2/3 of cortex.
evidence: Speculative generalization from the observed pattern

claim: AM responses in ACx appear to be more sustained than VM mismatch responses in visual cortex.
source: Specifically, AM responses in ACx (Figure 2D) appear to be more sustained than VM mismatch responses in visual cortex.
evidence: Inferred from comparison of response time courses

claim: Sound playback halt responses in ACx are very weak.
source: Additionally, unlike the observed visual flow playback halt responses in V1 and their increase during running (Vasilevskaya et al., 2023), we found only very weak responses to sound playback halts and no evidence of an influence of running on these responses (Figure 2—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing weak responses

claim: The mouse generates additional sounds while running on an air-supported treadmill that correlate with running speed intensity.
source: A decreased dependence of playback halt responses on running may be caused by the fact that the mouse generates additional sounds while running on an air-supported treadmill (e.g., treadmill rotation, changes in airflow, footsteps). These sounds correlate with running speed intensity and may reduce the relative salience of sound playback halts during running.
evidence: Speculative explanation for observed differences

claim: Additional sounds generated during running may reduce the relative salience of sound playback halts during running.
source: These sounds correlate with running speed intensity and may reduce the relative salience of sound playback halts during running.
evidence: Speculative explanation for observed pattern

claim: Differences in the experimental control of the sensorimotor coupling for different sensory modalities could account for some of the observed differences between the AM and VM mismatch responses.
source: Thus, differences in the experimental control of the sensorimotor coupling for a different sensory modalities could account for some of the observed differences between the AM and VM mismatch responses.
evidence: Speculative explanation for observed differences

claim: A similar non-linear relationship between auditory and visual oddball responses has been described in both ACx and V1.
source: A similar non-linear relationship has been described between auditory and visual oddball responses in both ACx and V1 (Shiramatsu et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work

claim: Deviations from linearity in terms of spiking responses are difficult to assess using calcium imaging data.
source: At this point, it should be kept in mind that deviations from linearity in terms of spiking responses are difficult to assess using calcium imaging data.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge about limitations of calcium imaging

claim: The underlying spiking responses to concurrent mismatches are likely non-linear.
source: However, given that the difference between the concurrent presentation and the linear sum of the two individual mismatch responses was approximately a factor of two (Figure 4E), and the fact that we found a population of neurons that responds selectively to the concurrent presentation of both mismatches, we suspect that also the underlying spiking responses are non-linear.
evidence: Inferred from the magnitude of the effect and selective responses

claim: Neurons in ACx have access to information about VM mismatches from at least two sources.
source: What are the mechanisms that could underlie this interaction? Neurons in ACx have access to information about VM mismatches from at least two sources.
evidence: Inferred from known anatomy and physiology

claim: VM mismatch responses are detectable across most of dorsal cortex in widefield calcium imaging.
source: In widefield calcium imaging, VM mismatch responses are detectable across most of dorsal cortex (Heindorf and Keller, 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work

claim: VM mismatch responses are present in long-range cortico-cortical axons from V1, or possibly in L4, L5, or L6 neurons in ACx.
source: Thus, we speculate that VM mismatch responses are present in long-range cortico-cortical axons from V1, or possibly in L4, L5, or L6 neurons in ACx.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of potential mechanisms

claim: Locus coeruleus drives noradrenergic signals in response to VM mismatches across the entire dorsal cortex.
source: Locus coeruleus, for example, drives noradrenergic signals in response to VM mismatches across the entire dorsal cortex (Jordan and Keller, 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work

claim: Noradrenergic signals only weakly modulate responses in L2/3 neurons in V1.
source: However, given that noradrenergic signals only weakly modulate responses in L2/3 neurons in V1 (Jordan and Keller, 2023), it is unclear if the broadcasted noradrenergic signals could non-linearly potentiate the AM mismatch responses of ACx neurons.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work

claim: It is unclear if broadcasted noradrenergic signals could non-linearly potentiate the AM mismatch responses of ACx neurons.
source: However, given that noradrenergic signals only weakly modulate responses in L2/3 neurons in V1 (Jordan and Keller, 2023), it is unclear if the broadcasted noradrenergic signals could non-linearly potentiate the AM mismatch responses of ACx neurons.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about potential mechanisms

claim: Cholinergic signals are unlikely to contribute to the multimodal mismatch effect.
source: We speculate that cholinergic signals are also unlikely to contribute to this effect.
evidence: Speculative reasoning about potential mechanisms

claim: There are no cholinergic responses to VM mismatch in V1.
source: In V1 there are no cholinergic responses to VM mismatch (Yogesh and Keller, 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work

claim: ACx and V1 receive cholinergic innervation from different sources.
source: However, given that ACx and V1 receive cholinergic innervation from different sources (Kim et al., 2016), we cannot rule out the possibility that cholinergic signals in ACx respond to VM mismatch.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior work

claim: The possibility that cholinergic signals in ACx respond to VM mismatch cannot be ruled out.
source: However, given that ACx and V1 receive cholinergic innervation from different sources (Kim et al., 2016), we cannot rule out the possibility that cholinergic signals in ACx respond to VM mismatch.
evidence: Acknowledges uncertainty about cholinergic contribution

claim: [AM + VM] mismatch responses are primarily driven by long-range cortico-cortical input from V1 that interacts with a local computation of [AM] mismatch responses in the L2/3 ACx circuit.
source: In sum, given that the [AM + VM] mismatch responses do not simply appear to be an amplified variant of the [AM] mismatch responses (Figure 4F), we speculate that [AM + VM] mismatch responses are primarily driven by long-range cortico-cortical input from V1 that interacts with a local computation of [AM] mismatch responses in the L2/3 ACx circuit.
evidence: Speculative interpretation of the mechanism

claim: Lateral interactions in the computation of prediction errors between sensory streams are not accounted for by hierarchical variants of predictive processing.
source: Lateral interactions in the computation of prediction errors between sensory streams are not accounted for by hierarchical variants of predictive processing.
evidence: Inferred from theoretical framework of hierarchical predictive processing

claim: New variants of predictive processing models that include lateral and non-hierarchical interactions are needed to explain the lateral interactions between prediction errors in ACx and V1.
source: To explain the lateral interactions between prediction errors likely computed in ACx (AM mismatch responses) and prediction errors likely computed in V1 (VM mismatch responses) that we describe here, we will need new variants of predictive processing models that include lateral and non-hierarchical interactions.
evidence: Inferred from the incompatibility of findings with hierarchical models

claim: Mismatch responses in different modalities interact non-linearly and can potentiate each other.
source: Thus, our results demonstrate that mismatch responses in different modalities interact non-linearly and can potentiate each other.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing super-additive responses

claim: The circuit mechanisms that underlie multimodal integration of mismatch responses are still unclear and will require further investigation.
source: The circuit mechanisms that underlie this form of multimodal integration of mismatch responses are still unclear and will require further investigation.
evidence: Acknowledges gap in current understanding

claim: Unimodal and hierarchical variants of predictive processing are insufficient to explain cortical mismatch responses.
source: However, we would argue that the relatively strong multimodal interaction demonstrates that unimodal and hierarchical variants of predictive processing are insufficient to explain cortical mismatch responses – if predictive processing aims to be a general theory of cortical function, we will need to explore non-hierarchical variants of predictive processing.
evidence: Inferred from the observed multimodal interactions

claim: If predictive processing aims to be a general theory of cortical function, we will need to explore non-hierarchical variants of predictive processing.
source: However, we would argue that the relatively strong multimodal interaction demonstrates that unimodal and hierarchical variants of predictive processing are insufficient to explain cortical mismatch responses – if predictive processing aims to be a general theory of cortical function, we will need to explore non-hierarchical variants of predictive processing.
evidence: Inferred from the limitations of hierarchical models in explaining the data

claim: Prediction errors can be potentiated by multimodal interactions in primary sensory cortices.
source: Overall, our results demonstrate that prediction errors can be potentiated by multimodal interactions in primary sensory cortices.
evidence: Supported by experimental data showing amplified responses to concurrent mismatches

claim: C57BL/6 female mice between the ages of 7 and 12 weeks were used in this study.
source: C57BL/6 female mice (Charles River), between the ages of 7 and 12 weeks were used in this study.
evidence: Describes the experimental subjects

claim: Mice underwent a cranial window implantation surgery at an age of between 7 and 8 weeks.
source: Mice underwent a cranial window implantation surgery at an age of between 7 and 8 weeks.
evidence: Describes the experimental procedure

claim: The delay in the AM closed loop coupling was 260 ± 60 ms (mean ± STD).
source: This closed loop coupling was not instantaneous but exhibited a delay of 260 ± 60 ms (mean ± STD).
evidence: Describes a technical parameter of the experimental setup

claim: The delay in the VM closed loop coupling was 90 ± 10 ms (mean ± STD).
source: The delay in the VM closed loop coupling was 90 ± 10 ms (mean ± STD).
evidence: Describes a technical parameter of the experimental setup

claim: The study recorded from 7637 neurons in 17 mice.
source: In one to six recording sessions, 1 session per day, we recorded from 7637 neurons in 17 mice.
evidence: Describes the sample size of the study

claim: VM mismatch responses are likely calculated in V1.
source: VM mismatch responses are likely calculated in V1 (Jordan and Keller, 2020), and spread across dorsal cortex from there (Heindorf and Keller, 2023).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior work
